title: Bhima in the dancing hall
hookLine: in the middle of the night Draupadi goes to the kitchen, wakes the cook, and tells him everything
carry: a protector's dharma: stop the cruelty

cards: It's night in King Virata's palace. Draupadi can't sleep. She gets up, crosses the dark courtyard, and goes to the kitchen, where the royal cook Vallava is asleep.
She doesn't go to Yudhishthira. She goes to Bhima. She wakes him, and the first thing she says is a question: how can you sleep?

teach.b: Then she tells him all of it, and the epic gives her room. Not only Kichaka.

The whole road: the dice hall, the forest, a queen grinding sandal paste for another queen until her hands are rough, the king of the world playing dice for a living. She's grieving for all of them. And Bhima listens.
The text says he holds her hands and weeps with her. Then the cook makes a plan. Tell Kichaka yes, he says.

teach.h: A MEETING IN THE DANCING HALL
teach.b: Meet him tonight in the dancing hall, empty after dark. I'll be waiting instead. Kichaka arrives dressed for a meeting and finds the cook.

They fight, two strong men in an empty hall, and Bhima kills him. The court blames the hidden Gandharvas. When Kichaka's kinsmen turn on Sairandhri, Bhima rescues her again, and still nobody names the cook.
Now the teaching. Yesterday Yudhishthira held back; tonight Bhima acts.
Hindus prize ahimsa, not harming, but the Mahabharata never makes that mean standing by while someone is hurt. A warrior's dharma is protection.
The poet Kalidasa explains the warrior's very name, kshatra, as the one who saves others from harm. Bhima is disguised as a cook, but his dharma isn't. Today most of us aren't warriors.
Still, a protector's dharma asks something of anyone: when someone is being hurt and you can stop it or bring help, you step in, after you've listened.

how: The killing of Kichaka is staged in dance-drama traditions such as Kathakali, and the night conversation between Draupadi and Bhima is retold as a scene of grief and loyalty.

o: the cook who meets Kichaka in the dancing hall
the Matsya king whose palace still hides the Pandavas
a heavenly guardian blamed for Kichaka's death

games.q: the night in the palace — tap the pairs.
p: crossed to the kitchen at night
wept with her, then made a plan

s: Draupadi went to Yudhishthira for help that night
she went to the kitchen and woke Bhima, the cook Vallava.
the trap was set in the dancing hall
the hall where the princesses learned dance by day stood empty at night.
in Hindu teaching, ahimsa means never stepping in to stop harm
the epic holds both: not harming, and a protector's duty to stop cruelty.

games.q: you're Bhima. Draupadi has woken you in the kitchen and told you everything. what do you say first?
o: let's wake Yudhishthira and ask permission.
hold her hands, weep with her, then plan to meet Kichaka in the dancing hall.
march to Kichaka's house right now.
games.why: he listens and weeps with her first. then he plans: protection is his dharma, even disguised as a cook.

practice: Rest your hands palm up in your lap, the way Bhima held Draupadi's. Bring to mind someone who's had a hard week. Breathing in, simply listen, in your mind, to what they might say.
Breathing out, ask what protecting them would look like: a call, a word, standing beside them. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Virata. The palace where a cook keeps a promise in an empty dancing hall, and the disguise survives the night.

carryVoice: Your line: a protector's dharma: stop the cruelty. He held her hands before he made a plan. Day eight hundred ten, done.
